question: A patient with Clostridioides difficile diarrhoea is being discharged. Which agent should be used to decontaminate the room's environmental surfaces?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. C. difficile produces highly resistant endospores. Sodium hypochlorite at 1% (10,000 ppm) is sporicidal and is the recommended agent for terminal cleaning of C. difficile rooms.

Alcohol is not sporicidal — it acts by protein denaturation and lipid dissolution, neither of which penetrates the spore coat. C. difficile spores survive alcohol disinfection; this is also why alcohol hand rubs are inadequate (soap-and-water handwashing is required).

Quaternary ammonium compounds (e.g., benzalkonium chloride) are low-level disinfectants effective against vegetative bacteria but not against spores. They are unsuitable for C. difficile environmental decontamination.

While 0.1% (1,000 ppm) sodium hypochlorite is adequate for routine surface disinfection, this concentration is insufficient for spore elimination. C. difficile decontamination requires the higher sporicidal concentration of 1% (10,000 ppm).

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: C. difficile forms endospores, so you need a sporicidal agent. Most common disinfectants (alcohol, quaternary ammonium compounds) are not sporicidal. Sodium hypochlorite at 1% (10,000 ppm) is the standard sporicidal agent for environmental decontamination.

C. difficile spores resist alcohol and quaternary ammonium compounds. High-concentration sodium hypochlorite (1% = 10,000 ppm) is sporicidal and is the standard for terminal cleaning. Also remember: handwashing with soap and water (not alcohol rub) for C. difficile.
